title: Match Text Against a Small Pattern Language
constraints: text contains lowercase letters; pattern contains lowercase letters, . and *

examples.explanation: a, then b* matches bbb, then c.
a.* can match `abc`, but then the pattern still needs a `d`.

hints.nudge: Look at the first element of the pattern. If it is followed by a `*` there are two choices: use it zero times, or use it once and keep the same pattern element for the rest. What does that remind you of?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over prefixes: match[i][j] is true if the first i letters of the text match the first j elements of the pattern; handle `*` by either dropping the 'element*' pair, or consuming one letter and staying on the same element.
hints.pseudocode:
match[0][0] = true; for j: if pattern[j - 1] == '*': match[0][j] = match[0][j - 2]
for i, j: if pattern[j - 1] == '*': match[i][j] = match[i][j - 2] or (letterFits(text[i - 1], pattern[j - 2]) and match[i - 1][j])
          else: match[i][j] = letterFits(text[i - 1], pattern[j - 1]) and match[i - 1][j - 1]
return match[len(text)][len(pattern)]
(letterFits(a, p) is true when p == '.' or p == a)
hints.walkthrough: A plain recursion branches at every `*` and repeats the same (position in the text, position in the pattern) pairs, which is exponential. There are only (len(text) + 1) * (len(pattern) + 1) such pairs, so tabulate them. A pair (i, j) is about the first i letters and the first j pattern characters. If the last pattern character is a letter or a dot, the last text letter must fit it and the earlier parts must match. If it is a star, the element before it (pattern[j - 2]) can be used zero times (the star pair disappears: match[i][j - 2]) or at least once (the last text letter fits that element and the text without it still matches the SAME pattern: match[i - 1][j]). The empty text can match a pattern only if it is made of `x*` pairs. O(len(text) * len(pattern)).
